newsitem.title: UK: Traders quickly adapt to daily LME stock reporting.
newsitem.headline: Traders quickly adapt to daily LME stock reporting.

text.p: The start of daily reporting of London Metal Exchange (LME) stocks held in approved warehouses from April 7 held few surprises for traders and market analysts.
In March the LME said the main advantage of daily reporting, as opposed to twice weekly reports on Tuesdays and Fridays, would be the enhanced transparency brought to stock levels and movements.

A greater transparency of inventories was among the recommendations put forward by the Securities and Investments Boards (SIB) in its in depth review of the workings of the LME and the metals markets.
Stocks will be reported daily for an initial six month trial period.
LME floor traders have quickly adapted to daily reporting and now see it as normal. Some said the data will cease to have much impact unless there is a sharp move on a particular day.
Others noted that the cumulative effect of a run of movements would be muted, so overall market volatility and trading opportunities would be lost.
"If something falls a 1,000 tonnes every day you tend to forget it. But over a week that is 7,000 tonnes. If stocks drop that much in one report the market reacts," one said.
Over the past week traders and analysts appraised the movements of stocks in and out of LME warehouses.
Total copper stocks fell by 14,800 tonnes, tin by 150 tonnes and aluminium by 6,775 tonnes. Alloy fell by 1,080, while zinc declined by 1,400 tonnes.
Both nickel and lead rose by 972 tonnes and 900 tonnes respectively.
"Stocks have been in decline this year which is a reflection of the overall strengthening global economies," Martin Squires of Rudolf Wolff said.
Squires said the exception has been copper which may be a surprise to many market operators.

This has been largely attributed to concerns over the potential for renewed Chinese stockpiling and because stock levels are still at historical lows. Year-to-date copper stocks have risen by 34,325 tonnes, a increase of 27.4 percent.
The increases in copper stocks were seen in the first two months of 1997.
Squires said since February 20 stocks have fallen by 28 percent or 62,500 tonnes, of which 27,175 tonnes was out of Singapore.
This highlights regional strength which is attributed to Japanese GSP and trade purchases in anticipation of Chinese re-stocking.
In the other regions where stock drawdowns have been seen there has been a show of underlying economic strength.
The narrowing of copper's cash to three months spread from over a $300 backwardation at one stage, deterred trade buying which preferred to operate on a hand to mouth basis.
But with the easing and signals of favourable economic conditions in most regions copper stocks are likely to decline.
"We expect stocks to be further drawn down in the coming weeks. In turn this could lead to further price spikes and a jump in market volatility," Squires said.
